breakfast.name: Lu Sipi (Lamb in Taro Leaves)
instructions: Layer taro leaves, lamb, onion, coconut cream
Wrap in banana leaves or foil
Bake 2 hours until tender
breakfast.description: Lamb slow-cooked in taro leaves with coconut cream.

breakfast.name: Manioke (Boiled Cassava)
instructions: Boil cassava until tender
Serve with coconut cream

breakfast.name: Taro Porridge
instructions: Taro is the staple starch of Tonga -- eaten at every meal
As a breakfast: taro cooked and mashed with coconut milk
Sweetened with honey or sugar
A warm, nourishing start to the day
breakfast.description: Tongan taro breakfast porridge -- taro mashed with warm coconut milk and sweetened with honey. Taro is the fundamental Tongan starch. A warm, nourishing breakfast.

breakfast.name: Faiai Eleni (Spinach in Coconut Milk)
ingredients: Taro leaves or spinach (or island greens)
instructions: Faiai eleni is the Tongan coconut cream spinach -- a simple, common dish
Greens cooked in thick coconut milk
The coconut milk makes the greens rich and silky
A standard side dish or breakfast component
Taro leaves are traditional but spinach is used as a substitute
breakfast.description: Tongan coconut cream greens -- taro leaves or spinach cooked in thick coconut milk until silky. Faiai eleni is a standard side dish or breakfast component. Coconut cream transforms the greens.

lunch.name: Ota Ika (Raw Fish Salad)
instructions: Marinate tuna in lime 15 min
Add coconut cream
Toss with vegetables
lunch.description: Tongan raw fish in coconut and lime.

lunch.name: Umu (Earth Oven) Meats
instructions: Heat stones
Wrap food in banana leaves
Layer over hot stones
Cover with earth, cook 3 hours

lunch.name: Lu Pulu (Taro Leaf with Corned Beef)
ingredients: Corned beef (canned -- introduced by European traders)
instructions: Lu pulu is one of Tonga's most popular dishes
Taro leaves stuffed with corned beef and onion
Wrapped in more taro leaves
Cooked in coconut milk until everything is silky
Or cooked in an umu (underground oven)
Corned beef: introduced by European traders -- became embedded in Polynesian cooking
The combination of taro leaf and canned corned beef is distinctly Pacific
lunch.description: Tongan taro leaf parcel with corned beef -- taro leaves wrapped around corned beef (introduced by European traders) and onion, cooked in coconut milk until silky. Corned beef became embedded in Polynesian cooking after European contact. The taro leaf and canned beef combination is distinctly Pacific.

lunch.name: Ota Ika (Raw Fish Salad)
ingredients: Fresh fish (snapper, tuna, or similar -- very fresh)
Lime juice (generous -- to cure the fish)
instructions: Ota ika is the Tongan and wider Pacific raw fish salad
The fish is cut into pieces and marinated in lime juice until the flesh turns opaque
The acid "cooks" the fish -- the protein denatures from the lime acid
Then coconut milk is added -- it turns the dish creamy and mild
Tomato, cucumber, and spring onion complete the salad
Closely related to Fijian kokoda and other Pacific raw fish dishes
lunch.description: Tongan raw fish salad -- fresh fish cured in lime juice (the acid denatures the protein), then coconut milk added to make it creamy, with tomato, cucumber, and spring onion. Related to Fijian kokoda and Pacific raw fish traditions across Polynesia.

lunch.name: Kapisi Pulu (Cabbage in Coconut Cream)
instructions: Kapisi pulu is the Tongan cabbage cooked in coconut cream
Similar to lu pulu but with cabbage instead of taro leaves
Cabbage was introduced through European contact
Now part of the Tongan staple diet
Cooked until very soft in thick coconut cream
lunch.description: Tongan cabbage in coconut cream -- shredded cabbage (European introduction) with corned beef or tuna cooked in thick coconut cream until soft. Part of the post-contact Tongan diet that blended indigenous ingredients with introduced foods.

dinner.name: Lupulu (Corned Beef in Taro Leaves)
instructions: Layer taro leaves with corned beef, onion, coconut cream
Wrap and bake 1 hour
dinner.description: Corned beef wrapped in taro leaves.

imageCredit.author: No machine-readable author provided. Hagen Graebner assumed (based on copyright claims).

dinner.name: Grilled Fish
instructions: Season fish, grill over coals
Serve with coconut cream and root vegetables

dinner.name: Umu (Underground Oven Feast)
ingredients: Taro leaves, banana leaves (for wrapping and layering)
instructions: Umu is the Polynesian earth oven -- the method for the traditional feast
A pit is dug and lined with volcanic stones
A fire is lit to heat the stones until they are very hot
The food is wrapped in banana and taro leaves
Placed on the hot stones, covered with more leaves and earth
Cooked for 2-4 hours in the steam and heat
The umu is for celebrations: weddings, funerals, first birthdays, and national events
Opening the umu is a ceremony -- the smell that escapes is part of the event
dinner.description: Tongan earth oven feast -- a pit lined with volcanic stones heated by fire, food wrapped in banana and taro leaves placed on the hot stones, covered and steamed for 2-4 hours. The umu is used for celebrations: weddings, funerals, and national events. Opening the umu is a ceremony.

dinner.name: Faikakai Topai (Sweet Dumplings in Coconut Syrup)
ingredients: Coconut milk, sugar, vanilla (for the syrup)
instructions: Faikakai topai are the Tongan sweet dumplings in coconut syrup
Simple flour dumplings boiled until cooked
Served in a warm coconut-sugar syrup
A popular Tongan dessert or sweet snack
dinner.description: Tongan sweet dumplings -- simple flour dumplings boiled, served in warm coconut milk and sugar syrup. A popular dessert across Tonga.

dinner.name: Roasted Pig (Puaka Tunu)
ingredients: Whole small pig or large pork pieces
instructions: Roasted pig is central to Tongan feasts and celebrations
The whole pig is the symbol of feast and generosity
Roasted over coals or in the umu
The crackling: the prized part
Presented whole at celebrations -- the host's offering to guests
dinner.description: Tongan feast roast pig -- whole pig roasted over coals or in the umu. The whole pig is the symbol of Tongan feast and generosity. The crackling is the prized part. Presented whole as the host's offering to guests at celebrations.

snacks.name: Faikakai Topai (Dumplings in Coconut)
instructions: Make small dough balls
Boil until cooked
Toss in sweetened coconut cream

snacks.name: Fekei (Taro Cake)
instructions: Fekei is the Tongan steamed taro cake
Grated or mashed taro mixed with coconut milk and sugar
Steamed until set into a cake
Slightly sweet and dense
Eaten as a snack or dessert
snacks.description: Tongan steamed taro cake -- grated taro mixed with coconut milk and sugar, steamed until set into a dense, slightly sweet cake. Eaten as a snack or dessert.

snacks.name: Dried Fish
instructions: Dried fish is a traditional Tongan preservation method
Fish sun-dried and salted
Keeps without refrigeration
Eaten as a snack or added to other dishes for flavor
The preservation tradition of island life without refrigeration
snacks.description: Tongan sun-dried salted fish -- fish dried and salted for preservation. The traditional island preservation method before refrigeration. Eaten as a snack or added to dishes for flavor.

snacks.name: Coconut Cream (Served Fresh)
ingredients: Coconut water, coconut meat (scraped and pressed)
instructions: Fresh coconut cream is the Tongan flavor base -- pressed fresh and drunk or used in cooking
A young green coconut is drunk for the water
A mature brown coconut is scraped and pressed for cream
Drinking fresh coconut water from a green coconut is the Tongan refresher
The cream pressed from the mature coconut is the cooking fat and flavor of all Tongan food
snacks.description: Tongan fresh coconut cream -- pressed from mature coconut, the base of all Tongan cooking. Young coconut water drunk fresh. The coconut provides both the drink (young) and the cooking fat (mature). Central to Tongan food at every level.

desserts.name: Faikakai (Sweet Coconut Pudding)
instructions: Mix grated starch with coconut cream and sugar
Cook until thick
desserts.description: Sweet starchy pudding in coconut cream.

desserts.name: Banana Cake (Tongan Style)
ingredients: Coconut milk (in place of regular milk)
instructions: Banana cake with coconut milk is the Tongan home baking style
Ripe bananas mashed into a simple cake batter
Coconut milk gives the Pacific flavor
Baked until golden
A simple, home-baked treat
desserts.description: Tongan banana cake -- mashed ripe bananas in a simple cake with coconut milk for Pacific flavor. Home-baked and eaten as a sweet treat. Bananas and coconut are the Tongan pantry.

desserts.name: Haupia (Coconut Pudding)
instructions: Haupia is the Hawaiian and broader Polynesian coconut pudding
Coconut milk thickened with cornstarch into a firm, sliceable pudding
Eaten cold
Clean, pure coconut flavor
Served at celebrations in Tonga and across Polynesia
desserts.description: Tongan Polynesian coconut pudding -- haupia, coconut milk thickened with cornstarch until firm enough to slice, served cold. Pure, clean coconut flavor. Served at celebrations across Polynesia.

imageCredit.author: Arnold Gatilao from Fremont, CA, USA

drinks.name: Kava (Tongan Style)
instructions: Mix pounded kava with water
Strain through cloth
Serve in coconut shells
Clap before and after drinking
drinks.description: Ceremonial kava — Tonga's social and ritual drink.

drinks.name: Otai (Fruit Drink)
instructions: Grate or chop fruit finely
Mix with coconut cream and water
Add sugar
Serve cold
drinks.description: Chunky tropical fruit drink with coconut cream.

drinks.name: Kava (Tongan Ceremony)
ingredients: Kava root (Piper methysticum -- dried and ground or fresh and pounded)
Cold water (used to strain the kava through a cloth)
instructions: Kava is the Pacific ceremonial drink -- and it is most deeply embedded in Tonga
Made from the root of Piper methysticum (a pepper plant)
Pounded or ground, mixed with cold water, and strained through a cloth
The active compound: kavalactones -- mildly anxiolytic and muscle-relaxing
In Tonga, kava ceremony (faikava) is the central social ritual
Drunk from a coconut shell cup (ipu)
The kava circle: the king drinks first, then by rank
The ceremony is integral to Tongan politics, diplomacy, and daily social life
Tonga has the most elaborate and formal kava ceremony in the Pacific
drinks.description: Tongan ceremonial drink -- kava (Piper methysticum root), pounded and strained through cloth with cold water. Kavalactones: mildly anxiolytic and muscle-relaxing. In Tonga, kava ceremony (faikava) is the central social ritual. Drunk by rank from a coconut shell (ipu). The king drinks first. Integral to Tongan politics and diplomacy.
